splits.legalQuestion: Whether a multiemployer pension plan actuary may select actuarial assumptions for calculating withdrawal liability after the statutory measurement date (the end of the prior plan year), or whether all such assumptions must be fixed by that date.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on when actuarial assumptions must be finalized for calculating employer withdrawal liability from multiemployer pension plans. This affects billions of dollars in potential obligations for thousands of employers participating in such plans, as the timing directly controls how much withdrawing employers must pay.

positions.label: Assumptions may be selected after measurement date
positions.summary: Holds that the plan actuary may select actuarial assumptions after the statutory measurement date, as the statute does not require all assumptions to be locked in by year-end.

circuits.name: Seventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund

positions.label: Assumptions must be fixed by measurement date
positions.summary: Holds that all actuarial assumptions must be fixed by the statutory measurement date (end of the prior plan year), providing employers greater predictability about potential liability.

circuits.name: Fifth Circuit
circuits.caseName: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund

splits.relatedScotusTitle: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the term of supervised release is tolled (paused) when a supervisee absconds from supervision, thereby extending the period during which the person can be found to have violated the conditions of supervised release.
splits.description: Circuits split on whether federal courts may apply a judicially-created 'fugitive tolling' doctrine to supervised release, effectively extending the supervision period beyond the time specified in the judgment when a person absconds. The outcome affects how courts calculate sentencing guidelines at revocation hearings for thousands of individuals who abscond each year.

positions.label: Tolling applies
positions.summary: Holds that the term of supervised release is tolled during the period a supervisee is a fugitive, allowing courts to find violations and revoke release even after the nominal term would have expired.

positions.label: Tolling does not apply
positions.summary: Holds that there is no statutory basis for tolling supervised release when a supervisee absconds, so the term expires as originally set regardless of absconding.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 2244(b)(1)'s bar on relitigating previously raised claims in habeas proceedings applies to federal prisoners filing motions under Section 2255.
splits.description: Circuits are split 6-to-3 on whether federal prisoners face a stricter gatekeeping requirement than Congress intended when bringing successive collateral attacks. If (b)(1) applies, federal prisoners are categorically barred from raising any claim they previously presented, in addition to Section 2255(h)'s requirements. If not, they need only satisfy 2255(h).

positions.label: Section 2244(b)(1) applies to § 2255 motions
positions.summary: Holds that the categorical bar on relitigating previously raised claims under § 2244(b)(1) applies to federal prisoners filing successive § 2255 motions, imposing an additional gatekeeping requirement.

positions.label: Section 2244(b)(1) does not apply to § 2255 motions
positions.summary: Holds that § 2244(b)(1) does not apply to federal prisoners filing § 2255 motions, so they need only satisfy § 2255(h)'s requirements of newly discovered evidence or a new rule of constitutional law.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a candidate for federal office has Article III standing to challenge a state law that allows the counting of mail-in ballots received after Election Day.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on the standard for evaluating whether candidates have standing to bring pre-election challenges to voting procedures. The outcome affects the ability to challenge mail-in voting rules, ballot counting deadlines, and other election administration practices nationwide.

positions.label: Broad candidate standing
positions.summary: Holds that candidates have standing to challenge election rules that allegedly dilute their votes or affect the electoral process, even before an election takes place.

positions.label: Narrow candidate standing
positions.summary: Holds that candidates must demonstrate a concrete, particularized injury to establish standing, and speculative pre-election claims are insufficient.

circuits.name: Seventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: Bost v. Illinois State Board of Elections

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Bost v. Illinois State Board of Elections

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the rule of lenity takes precedence over agency or Sentencing Commission deference (Auer/Kisor deference) when interpreting ambiguous criminal sentencing provisions.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether lenity trumps deference to agency interpretations in the criminal context. At least three circuits hold that lenity prevails, while the Third Circuit held that agency deference trumps lenity. The issue has gained importance after Loper Bright overruled Chevron deference.

positions.label: Lenity trumps deference
positions.summary: Holds that the rule of lenity takes precedence over deference to agency or Sentencing Commission interpretations when construing ambiguous criminal provisions, preventing agencies from expanding criminal liability.

positions.label: Deference trumps lenity
positions.summary: Holds that agency deference (Auer/Kisor deference) takes precedence over the rule of lenity when interpreting ambiguous sentencing guidelines, allowing the Sentencing Commission's commentary to control.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the word 'and' in the First Step Act's safety-valve provision, 18 U.S.C. § 3553(f)(1), is conjunctive (requiring all three criminal-history criteria to disqualify) or disjunctive (any one criterion disqualifies).
splits.description: Circuits are deeply split on whether a defendant must meet all three criminal-history criteria to be disqualified from safety-valve sentencing relief or whether possessing any single criterion is disqualifying. This affects whether defendants receive mandatory minimum sentences and implicates liberty interests and sentencing uniformity.

positions.label: 'And' is conjunctive — all three criteria required to disqualify
positions.summary: Holds that defendants are disqualified from safety-valve relief only if they meet all three criminal-history criteria listed in § 3553(f)(1), reading 'and' in its natural conjunctive sense.

positions.label: 'And' is disjunctive — any one criterion disqualifies
positions.summary: Holds that possessing any one of the three criminal-history criteria is sufficient to disqualify a defendant from safety-valve relief, reading 'and' as effectively meaning 'or.'

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Sentencing Guidelines commentary (Application Note 1) can expand the definition of 'controlled substance offense' under U.S.S.G. § 4B1.2(b) to include inchoate offenses like conspiracy, when the guideline text does not mention them.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether Application Note 1 to § 4B1.2 — which includes conspiracy and attempt within 'controlled substance offense' — is a valid, authoritative interpretation entitled to deference under Stinson/Kisor, or impermissibly expands the guideline beyond its text. The split affects career-offender designation for many defendants.

positions.label: Commentary is authoritative — inchoate offenses included
positions.summary: Holds that Application Note 1 is entitled to controlling weight as the Sentencing Commission's authoritative interpretation, and conspiracy qualifies as a controlled substance offense for career-offender purposes.

positions.label: Commentary cannot expand text — inchoate offenses excluded
positions.summary: Holds that the guideline text unambiguously excludes inchoate offenses and the commentary impermissibly expands the definition, so conspiracy does not qualify as a controlled substance offense for career-offender purposes.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a non-retroactive change in sentencing law, such as the First Step Act's anti-stacking amendment to 18 U.S.C. § 924(c), can constitute or contribute to 'extraordinary and compelling reasons' for compassionate release under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether non-retroactive changes in sentencing law may serve as a basis for compassionate release. The Eighth Circuit held in Crandall that such changes cannot contribute to extraordinary and compelling reasons, while the Seventh Circuit in Black addressed the Sentencing Commission's attempt to authorize such relief, finding the Commission exceeded its authority. Other circuits have been more receptive to considering such changes.

positions.label: Non-retroactive changes may support compassionate release
positions.summary: Holds that non-retroactive changes in sentencing law may be considered as part of the extraordinary and compelling reasons analysis, particularly when combined with other factors.

positions.label: Non-retroactive changes cannot support compassionate release
positions.summary: Holds that a non-retroactive change in law cannot contribute to a finding of extraordinary and compelling reasons for compassionate release, as this would circumvent Congress's decision not to make the change retroactive.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether post-petition, pre-conversion increases in the equity of a debtor's asset belong to the bankruptcy estate or to the debtor upon good-faith conversion from Chapter 13 to Chapter 7 under 11 U.S.C. § 348(f)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether appreciation in property value between filing for Chapter 13 bankruptcy and converting to Chapter 7 inures to the estate or remains with the debtor. The Ninth Circuit held that such appreciation belongs to the estate, creating a split with circuits that have held the appreciation belongs to the debtor.

positions.label: Appreciation belongs to the estate
positions.summary: Holds that the plain language of § 348(f)(1)(A), combined with the broad scope of § 541(a), means that any post-petition appreciation in property value belongs to the bankruptcy estate upon conversion.

positions.label: Appreciation belongs to the debtor
positions.summary: Holds that the Bankruptcy Code's structure and § 348(f)(1)(A)'s purpose establish that post-petition, pre-conversion appreciation belongs to the debtor in a good-faith conversion, not the estate.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the applicable time limit to appeal a Hyde Amendment order for attorney's fees in a criminal case is the civil deadline (30 days under Fed. R. App. P. 4(a)) or the criminal deadline (14 days under Fed. R. App. P. 4(b)).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether a Hyde Amendment motion for attorney's fees is a civil matter ancillary to the criminal case (triggering the 30-day deadline) or remains part of the criminal case (triggering the 14-day deadline). The Seventh Circuit joined the majority view applying the civil deadline, noting a lopsided circuit split.

positions.label: Civil deadline applies (30 days)
positions.summary: Holds that a Hyde Amendment motion is a civil matter ancillary to the criminal case, so the 30-day civil appeal deadline under Fed. R. App. P. 4(a) applies.

positions.label: Criminal deadline applies (14 days)
positions.summary: Holds that a Hyde Amendment motion remains part of the criminal proceedings, so the 14-day criminal appeal deadline under Fed. R. App. P. 4(b) applies.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a state drug conviction qualifies as a 'controlled substance offense' under the Sentencing Guidelines when the state schedule covers substances not listed in the federal Controlled Substances Act.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether the Guidelines' definition of 'controlled substance offense' requires the underlying substance to be federally controlled. The Eighth Circuit holds there is no federal-law limitation, while other circuits require a match to federal schedules. This affects career-offender and other sentencing enhancements for defendants with prior state drug convictions.

positions.label: No federal-schedule limitation
positions.summary: Holds that the Guidelines broadly define 'controlled substance offense' to include state law offenses regardless of whether the particular substance is controlled under federal law, finding no textual basis to graft a federal limitation.

positions.label: Federal-schedule match required
positions.summary: Holds that a state drug conviction qualifies as a controlled substance offense only if the substance at issue is also controlled under the federal Controlled Substances Act, applying a categorical approach.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a federal prisoner may use a habeas corpus petition under 28 U.S.C. § 2241 to challenge BOP decisions regarding earned time credits and transfer to prerelease custody under the First Step Act, or whether such claims must be brought through other means.
splits.description: Circuits have a longstanding and unresolved split on whether habeas corpus is the exclusive remedy for challenges to the fact or duration of confinement and whether claims about BOP prerelease custody decisions fall within habeas jurisdiction. The Eighth Circuit noted this 'unresolved conflict in the courts of appeals for more than half a century.' This affects thousands of federal prisoners seeking to enforce First Step Act time credit provisions.

positions.label: Habeas is available for such claims
positions.summary: Holds that habeas corpus under § 2241 is available to challenge BOP decisions about First Step Act time credits and prerelease custody transfers, as these challenges relate to the duration of confinement.

circuits.name: Third Circuit
circuits.caseName: Woodall v. Federal Bureau of Prisons

positions.label: Habeas is not available; use civil rights or APA claims
positions.summary: Holds that challenges to BOP transfer and custody decisions are challenges to conditions of confinement rather than the fact or duration of confinement, so habeas corpus is not the proper vehicle.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether district courts may expressly punish defendants for violations of supervised release conditions when revoking supervised release, or whether revocation sentences must be based solely on the breach of trust and the need to protect public safety.
splits.description: The Sixth Circuit's precedent in United States v. Lewis allows district courts to expressly punish defendants for supervised release violations, placing it at the extreme of a circuit split. Other circuits limit the purpose of revocation sentences to addressing the breach of the court's trust and protecting the public, not punishing the underlying violation conduct.

positions.label: Punishment for violations is permissible
positions.summary: Holds that district courts may impose revocation sentences that expressly punish defendants for their supervised release violations, in addition to addressing breach of trust.

positions.label: Punishment for violations is not the purpose
positions.summary: Holds that revocation sentences should be based on the breach of trust with the court and the need for deterrence and public protection, not punishment for the underlying violation conduct.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether an order denying a motion to seal documents containing private medical information is immediately appealable under the collateral order doctrine.
splits.description: The D.C. Circuit held that denial of a motion to seal medical records is immediately appealable as a collateral order because medical privacy is a value of 'high order,' but other circuits have been less receptive to extending the collateral order doctrine to sealing decisions. The question affects whether parties must wait until final judgment to challenge public disclosure of sensitive medical information.

positions.label: Immediately appealable
positions.summary: Holds that maintaining privacy in medical treatments and diagnoses is a value of high order warranting immediate appellate review under the collateral order doctrine, as delayed review risks irreparable loss of privacy.

positions.label: Not immediately appealable
positions.summary: Holds that orders denying motions to seal are not immediately appealable under the collateral order doctrine, as parties can seek review after final judgment or through mandamus.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a federal prisoner challenging BOP decisions regarding conditions of confinement, such as transfer to prerelease custody under the First Step Act, may bring a habeas corpus petition under 28 U.S.C. § 2241 or must pursue a civil rights action.
splits.description: A longstanding circuit split exists on whether challenges to conditions or execution of confinement — as opposed to the fact or duration of confinement — are cognizable as habeas claims under § 2241. This question affects federal prisoners seeking to enforce First Step Act time credits for earlier transfer to halfway houses or home confinement.

positions.label: Habeas is available for such claims
positions.summary: Holds that § 2241 habeas petitions are available to federal prisoners challenging BOP decisions about conditions or execution of confinement, including denials of earned time credit applications under the First Step Act.

circuits.name: Third Circuit
circuits.caseName: Woodall v. Federal Bureau of Prisons

positions.label: Habeas is not available; civil rights action required
positions.summary: Holds that challenges to conditions of confinement or BOP administrative decisions are not cognizable under § 2241 habeas and must be pursued through a civil rights action like a Bivens claim or the APA.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a trademark owner asserting a likelihood of confusion must demonstrate that consumers are likely to be confused at the time of purchase, or whether post-sale confusion experienced by third-party observers is sufficient to support a trademark infringement claim.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether post-sale confusion — confusion experienced by people who observe a product after it has been purchased, rather than by the purchaser at the point of sale — can independently support a trademark infringement claim. This affects how broadly trademark protection extends and has significant implications for luxury goods, fashion, and other industries.

positions.label: Post-sale confusion is sufficient
positions.summary: Holds that post-sale confusion among third-party observers, even without point-of-sale confusion, can support a trademark infringement claim because it harms the mark's distinctiveness and reputation.

circuits.name: Ninth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Au-Tomotive Gold Inc. v. Volkswagen of America

positions.label: Point-of-sale confusion is required
positions.summary: Holds that the relevant inquiry for trademark infringement is whether consumers are likely to be confused at the time of purchase, and that post-sale confusion alone is insufficient.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a noncitizen subject to a reinstated order of removal may challenge the legal basis for their detention through a habeas corpus petition in federal district court, or whether such challenges must be brought exclusively through the courts of appeals.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether federal district courts have jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. § 2241 to hear habeas challenges to detention by noncitizens subject to reinstated removal orders, or whether the immigration statutes channel all such challenges exclusively to the courts of appeals. This affects the procedural rights available to detained noncitizens.

positions.label: District court habeas is available
positions.summary: Holds that noncitizens subject to reinstated removal orders may challenge the legal basis for their detention through habeas petitions in federal district court under § 2241.

circuits.name: Third Circuit
circuits.caseName: Guerrero-Sanchez v. Warden York County Prison

positions.label: Challenges must go through courts of appeals
positions.summary: Holds that the immigration statutes channel all challenges to reinstated removal orders exclusively to the courts of appeals, stripping district courts of habeas jurisdiction.

splits.legalQuestion: What legal standards govern claims of discrimination or unfair treatment in the operation of hospitality or business establishments?
splits.description: The circuits have applied different standards for evaluating discrimination claims against business operators, creating uncertainty about liability and available remedies in hospitality, retail, and service industries. SCOTUS granted cert to resolve the disagreement.

positions.label: Broader liability standard
positions.summary: Applies a more expansive standard for establishing discrimination claims against business establishments, allowing broader theories of liability and damages.

positions.label: Narrower liability standard
positions.summary: Applies a more restrictive standard requiring stronger proof of discriminatory intent or conduct before imposing liability on business operators.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a state law categorically barring transgender women from women's sports teams violates the Equal Protection Clause as applied to transgender women who have medically mitigated sex-based biological advantages, and whether as-applied equal protection challenges are viable under intermediate scrutiny.
splits.description: Circuits are divided on whether categorical bans on transgender athlete participation survive intermediate scrutiny when applied to individuals who have undergone medical transition. The case also raises the broader question of whether sex-based classifications affecting transgender individuals warrant heightened scrutiny.

positions.label: Categorical ban violates Equal Protection as applied
positions.summary: Holds that a categorical ban fails intermediate scrutiny as applied to transgender women who have medically mitigated biological advantages, because the state has not shown the ban is substantially related to its interest in competitive fairness for this subclass.

positions.label: Categorical ban does not violate Equal Protection
positions.summary: Holds that biological sex-based classifications in athletics are substantially related to the important governmental interest in fair competition and the safety of female athletes, even as applied to transgender women.

circuits.name: Fourth Circuit
circuits.caseName: B.P.J. v. West Virginia State Board of Education

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Religious Land Use and Institutionalized Persons Act (RLUIPA) clearly authorizes individual-capacity damages suits against state prison officials, and whether Congress has the constitutional power under the Spending Clause to impose such personal liability.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether RLUIPA's text provides sufficiently clear notice to authorize damages claims against prison officials in their individual capacities, implicating Spending Clause limits on Congress's ability to impose personal liability on individuals who are not direct recipients of federal funds.

positions.label: RLUIPA authorizes individual-capacity damages
positions.summary: Holds that RLUIPA's text and structure provide clear authorization for damages suits against state prison officials in their individual capacities.

positions.label: RLUIPA does not authorize individual-capacity damages
positions.summary: Holds that RLUIPA does not clearly authorize individual-capacity damages suits against prison officials, and the Spending Clause limits Congress's ability to impose such liability on non-recipients of federal funds.

circuits.name: Fifth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Sossamon v. Lone Star State of Texas

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Landor v. Louisiana Department of Corrections and Public Safety

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a district court may consider factors related to potential errors or unfairness in a defendant's conviction or sentence as part of the 'extraordinary and compelling reasons' analysis for compassionate release under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether compassionate release motions may be used to raise claims that overlap with habeas corpus challenges, such as alleged sentencing errors or constitutional violations in the underlying conviction. Some circuits permit consideration of such factors, while others hold that § 3582(c)(1)(A) cannot be used as a substitute for § 2255 habeas relief.

positions.label: May consider conviction/sentence errors
positions.summary: Holds that district courts may consider legal errors or unfairness in a defendant's conviction or sentence as one factor in the extraordinary and compelling reasons analysis for compassionate release.

positions.label: Cannot use compassionate release for habeas-type claims
positions.summary: Holds that § 3582(c)(1)(A) is not an alternative avenue for claims properly raised under § 2255, and errors in conviction or sentencing cannot constitute extraordinary and compelling reasons for compassionate release.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Aviation Administration Authorization Act of 1994 (FAAAA) preempts state-law negligence claims against freight brokers who arrange transportation of property by motor carriers.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether the FAAAA's broad preemption clause, which prohibits states from enacting laws 'related to a price, route, or service of any... broker,' preempts common-law negligence claims against freight brokers for injuries arising from the carrier's operations. This split affects the liability exposure of freight brokers nationwide.

positions.label: FAAAA preempts broker negligence claims
positions.summary: Holds that state-law negligence claims against freight brokers are preempted by the FAAAA because they relate to the broker's services in arranging transportation.

circuits.name: Ninth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Miller v. C.H. Robinson Worldwide, Inc.

positions.label: FAAAA does not preempt broker negligence claims
positions.summary: Holds that state-law negligence claims against freight brokers are not preempted by the FAAAA because they are generally applicable common-law duties rather than regulations targeting broker services.

circuits.name: Eleventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Insecticide, Fungicide, and Rodenticide Act (FIFRA) preempts state-law failure-to-warn claims based on allegedly inadequate product labeling when the EPA has not required the specific warning.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether FIFRA's preemption provision bars state-law failure-to-warn claims against pesticide manufacturers when the claim is based on the absence of a warning that the EPA did not require. The split affects product liability litigation involving agricultural chemicals and consumer pesticide products.

positions.label: FIFRA preempts failure-to-warn claims
positions.summary: Holds that FIFRA preempts state-law failure-to-warn claims that would effectively require labeling different from or in addition to what FIFRA and EPA regulations permit.

positions.label: FIFRA does not preempt failure-to-warn claims
positions.summary: Holds that FIFRA does not preempt state-law failure-to-warn claims because such claims impose requirements 'parallel to' rather than 'in addition to' FIFRA's labeling requirements.

circuits.name: Third Circuit
circuits.caseName: DeKalb Genetics Corp. v. Bayer CropScience

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Monsanto Company v. John L. Durnell

splits.legalQuestion: Whether 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(3), which prohibits unlawful users of controlled substances from possessing firearms, violates the Second Amendment as applied to marijuana users.
splits.description: Following the Supreme Court's decision in Bruen, circuits have split on whether § 922(g)(3)'s prohibition on firearm possession by users of controlled substances — particularly marijuana — is constitutional. Some circuits have upheld the law under historical tradition analysis, while others have found it unconstitutional as applied to marijuana users.

positions.label: Section 922(g)(3) is constitutional
positions.summary: Holds that § 922(g)(3)'s prohibition on firearm possession by unlawful drug users is consistent with the nation's historical tradition of firearm regulation and survives Second Amendment scrutiny.

positions.label: Section 922(g)(3) is unconstitutional as applied
positions.summary: Holds that § 922(g)(3) violates the Second Amendment as applied to marijuana users because the government has not demonstrated a historical tradition of disarming persons who use intoxicating substances.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether workers who distribute baked goods to retail stores qualify as 'transportation workers engaged in foreign or interstate commerce' under Section 1 of the Federal Arbitration Act, thereby exempting them from mandatory arbitration agreements.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on the scope of the FAA's Section 1 transportation worker exemption, specifically whether workers who distribute goods to retail stores as part of a broader interstate distribution chain are 'transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce.' The split affects the enforceability of arbitration agreements for a broad class of last-mile delivery workers.

positions.label: Broad interpretation — last-mile workers exempt
positions.summary: Holds that workers who distribute goods to retail stores as part of an interstate distribution chain are transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce exempt from the FAA.

positions.label: Narrow interpretation — last-mile workers not exempt
positions.summary: Holds that workers who merely distribute goods locally to retail stores are not transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce and remain subject to FAA arbitration agreements.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 47(b) of the Investment Company Act creates a private right of action allowing parties to a contract that violates the ICA to sue in federal court for rescission of that contract.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether § 47(b) of the ICA provides an implied private right of action for rescission of contracts made in violation of the Act. This affects the ability of private parties to enforce the ICA's protections against abusive investment company practices through direct federal court actions.

positions.label: Section 47(b) creates a private right of action
positions.summary: Holds that § 47(b) creates an implied private right of action for rescission of contracts that violate the Investment Company Act, allowing private parties to sue directly.

circuits.name: Second Circuit
circuits.caseName: FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund

positions.label: Section 47(b) does not create a private right of action
positions.summary: Holds that § 47(b) is a voidability provision rather than a private right of action, and only the SEC can enforce the ICA's prohibitions.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act, as construed under the Gingles framework, can constitutionally compel race-based redistricting as a remedy for vote dilution, and whether compliance with Section 2 constitutes a compelling governmental interest justifying the use of race in drawing district lines.
splits.description: This case raises the question of whether race-conscious redistricting mandated by Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act is constitutionally permissible under the Equal Protection Clause. Lower courts have applied the Gingles framework to require consideration of race, but the constitutionality of this framework as applied is increasingly contested.

positions.label: Section 2 compels constitutionally permissible race-conscious redistricting
positions.summary: Holds that compliance with Section 2 of the VRA, as interpreted under the Gingles framework, constitutes a compelling interest that justifies the use of race in drawing district lines.

positions.label: Section 2's compelled race-based redistricting raises constitutional concerns
positions.summary: Holds or suggests that the Gingles framework's requirement of race-based redistricting may exceed constitutional limits under the Equal Protection Clause, particularly after Dobbs-era equal protection jurisprudence.

circuits.name: Eighth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Arkansas State Conference of the NAACP v. Arkansas Board of Apportionment
